question: Prato District Court has awarded a Senegalese worker family allowances arrears for nine children living in Senegal who were born from partnerships other than his marriage recognised in Italy. The case highlights the serious shortcomings inherent in a European regulatory framework that, under the auspices of the principle of equal treatment, restricts Member States’ autonomy in managing their social benefits.

Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2024/1233 and the case-law of the Court of Justice impose significant constraints on national laws. This creates a clear paradox: family situations resulting from polygamous unions – which are not recognised by Italian law – can nevertheless have an economic impact on the country’s social welfare system through the recognition of children’s rights. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission believe that it is acceptable for the current EU rules on equal treatment to have such an economic impact, limiting Member States’ ability to apply their own criteria on family benefits?
Will it consider revising Directive (EU) 2024/1233 to give Member States greater autonomy in regulating family benefits, including in situations arising from polygamous unions?
